sources.title: Roof coverings on historic buildings (web page)
sources.publisher: Babergh and Mid Suffolk District Councils
sources.verification: Re-fetched 2026-10-27 (M3.5) from https://www.babergh.gov.uk/roof-coverings-on-historic-buildings (HTTP 200; page title 'Roof coverings'; no date shown, footer (c) 2026); the excerpts below match that page's 'Traditional roof materials' section. A human should still re-read it in a browser at G1.

claims.text: Older timber-framed buildings in these districts were probably roofed originally with thatch or oak shingles, depending on which materials were available.

evidence.excerpt: Older timber framed buildings would probably have been roofed originally with either thatch or oak shingles depending on the whether materials were available.
Older, timber framed buildings would probably have been originally roofed with either thatch or oak shingles, depending on which materials were available.

claims.interpretation: Hedged ('probably'); local availability determined the original covering. Oak shingles are not modelled.
claims.visual_implications: Thatch state shown as the example older covering; narration keeps 'probably'.

claims.text: Longstraw thatch is the most typical / most traditional thatch in these districts and is laid at a steep pitch of about 50 degrees.

evidence.excerpt: Most typical for our districts is longstraw thatch, which is laid at the steeper pitch of about 50º.
Longstraw thatch is the most traditional material found in our districts and should be retained - having a characteristically steeper pitch of about 50ᵒ.

claims.interpretation: PDF says 'most typical', web page 'most traditional'; narration uses 'most traditional'. 'About' 50 degrees is approximate.
claims.visual_implications: thatch_50: 50-degree gable, thick (0.30 m) soft-edged covering, plain rounded ridge (SRC_002: thatch ridges traditionally plain).
claims.context: SRC_001 p. 9 also: 'In the north of Suffolk along the Waveney valley, water reed, usually capped with sedge, is more common.'

claims.text: Clay peg tiles eventually replaced some of the thatched roofs.

evidence.excerpt: Clay peg tiles eventually replaced some of these examples.
Eventually, clay peg tiles replaced some of our thatched roofs.

claims.interpretation: 'Some', not all: no universal sequence is implied.
claims.visual_implications: REPLACE_PARTS thatch_50 -> plain_tile_50 swaps only the covering; the structure stays (illustrative).

claims.text: Most plain clay tile roofs here are fairly steeply pitched, between 45 and 60 degrees.

evidence.excerpt: Most plain tile roofs are fairly steeply pitched between 45° and 60°, often replacing a former thatch covering.
In our districts, they are made of red or orange clay and are found on fairly steeply pitched between roofs of about 45ᵒ.

claims.interpretation: DISCREPANCY: PDF '45-60 degrees' (detailed guidance), web page 'about 45 degrees' (garbled sentence). M3.5 narration follows the PDF range; M3's open-ended '45 degrees or more' was not stated by either source.
claims.visual_implications: plain_tile_50 reuses the 50-degree structure (inside the PDF range); covering: thin slab with course lines every 0.115 m, half-round ridge (SRC_002: rounded red clay ridge tiles on tiled roofs).
claims.text_m3: Plain clay tile roofs there are fairly steeply pitched, typically about 45 degrees or more.

claims.text: From the eighteenth century, clay pantiles were used more commonly, once it became easier to move materials around the country.

evidence.excerpt: When it became easier to move materials around the country, clay pantiles would have been used more commonly in the 18th century, being transported by river or canal.
Clay pantiles were used more commonly from the eighteenth century onward ... once it became easier to move materials around the country, and they became cheaper.

claims.interpretation: DISCREPANCY: only the PDF mentions river/canal; only the web page mentions cost. Narration uses the shared part only.
claims.visual_implications: Pantiles are not modelled; mentioned on the 2D transport diagram only.

claims.text: In the nineteenth century, the railways meant that slate from Wales, Cornwall and Cumbria was often used in the area.

evidence.excerpt: In the 19th century, the creation of the railways meant that slate from Wales, Cornwall and Cumbria were often also used in our area.
In the nineteenth century, the creation of the railways meant that slate from Wales, Cornwall and Cumbria were often used in our area.

claims.interpretation: 'Often', not exclusively. Routes and quantities are not given; the diagram is schematic, not a map.
claims.visual_implications: Self-made schematic: three source labels with arrows to Suffolk, labelled 'schematic, not to scale'.

claims.text: Slate roofs there are usually pitched at around 30 degrees, and slate is more effective than other smaller tiles at a lower pitch.

evidence.excerpt: Slate is also on timber battens, but roofs are usually pitched at around 30º and are more effective than other smaller tiles at a lower pitch.
Roofs are normally pitched at around 30ᵒ, and are more effective than other smaller tiles at a lower pitch.

claims.interpretation: The sources state both facts side by side; they do not say the pitch was chosen *because* of this. Narration must not add 'because'.
claims.visual_implications: slate_30: own 30-degree structure; thin dark covering, course lines every 0.22 m, 'V' ridge (SRC_002: V-shaped ridge tiles more common on slate roofs).
claims.context: SRC_001 p. 11 also: 'A common feature in Suffolk is a plain tile roof with its lower courses above the eaves laid in slate ... usually at a shallower pitch' (coverings mixed on one building).

claims.text: Slates date from the 18th century onwards but are most common in the 19th century.

evidence.excerpt: They date from the 18th century onwards but are most common in the 19th century.

claims.interpretation: Single source. Not used in narration; kept to avoid implying slate only arrived with railways.

claims.text: US residential code minimum slopes by covering (Seattle 2012, IRC-based).
claims.interpretation: Out of scope for a Suffolk heritage story (different country, era and meaning: legal minimum vs historic typical pitch). Excluded by the M3 brief.

claims.text: Shirakawa-go gassho roofs are pitched above 60 degrees.
claims.interpretation: Primary source not readable (HTTP 403) and out of scope.

claims.text: Steep roofs exist because of snowfall or rainfall.
claims.interpretation: No source in scope supports a climate-causal claim; universal claims are excluded.
